description: Justice, peace and the work of CAFOD; Catholic mission and evangelism; the funeral rite and its meaning.
content_html:
Catholic Social Teaching: Loving Our Neighbour

Catholic Social Teaching (CST) is the set of principles through which the Church applies the Gospel to the structures of society. Its modern form emerged with Pope Leo XIII’s encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891) on workers’ rights, and has been developed by every subsequent Pope. CST’s core principles include the dignity of the human person, the common good, solidarity, subsidiarity (decisions at the lowest appropriate level), a preferential option for the poor, and care for creation.

The scriptural foundation for CST is the Sheep and Goats parable (Matthew 25:31–46). In this passage, Jesus describes the Last Judgment: those who fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked and visited the sick and imprisoned are told, “whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” Those who failed to act are condemned. This passage makes service of the poor not optional but a criterion of judgment.

Key Fact

Matthew 25:40: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” This is the foundational text for Catholic Social Teaching — serving the poor is not merely charity but an encounter with Christ himself. It gives CST its urgent moral character: justice for the vulnerable is not optional for Catholics.

CAFOD: Justice in Action

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the official overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales. It works in over forty countries, responding to humanitarian emergencies, funding long-term development projects, and campaigning for just global policies. CAFOD is motivated by Catholic Social Teaching and the belief that every person is made in the image of God and deserves a life of dignity.

CAFOD works in three areas: emergency relief (responding to disasters, conflicts and crises); long-term development (helping communities build sustainable livelihoods); and justice and advocacy (campaigning for fair trade, debt relief and climate justice). Catholics support CAFOD through annual fundraising events such as Fast Days and through parish giving.

Evangelii Gaudium and the Call to Action

Evangelii Gaudium (“The Joy of the Gospel”) was issued by Pope Francis in 2013. It is one of the key papal documents in the Edexcel specification. Francis calls the Church to be a “missionary Church” that goes to the margins rather than waiting for people to come to it. He writes that “the Gospel, radiant with the glory of Christ’s cross, constantly invites us to rejoice” and insists that the poor must be at the centre of the Church’s concern. The document connects mission directly to social justice: proclaiming the Gospel and serving the poor are inseparable.

Mission is the task given by the risen Jesus to his followers: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). The Catholic Church understands itself as fundamentally missionary — not in the sense of imposing its beliefs, but in the sense that it has something of immense value to share: the Good News of God’s love in Christ.

Evangelism (or evangelisation) takes many forms in British Catholic life today: running faith exploration courses (such as RCIA — the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults), speaking openly about faith, inviting others to Mass, engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths, and serving the poor as a witness to the Gospel. Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium insists that the Church must be a “missionary Church” that goes out, rather than remaining inward-looking.

Vincent Nichols and Catholic Leadership in England

Cardinal Vincent Nichols is the Archbishop of Westminster and the most senior Catholic leader in England and Wales. He was made a Cardinal by Pope Francis in 2014. He has been an outspoken voice on issues of social justice, poverty and the treatment of migrants and refugees, applying Catholic Social Teaching to contemporary British society. The Edexcel specification names him as an example of Catholic leadership in practice.

Key Fact

Evangelii Gaudium (Pope Francis, 2013): “The Joy of the Gospel.” Francis calls the Church to be a missionary community that goes to the margins and prioritises the poor. The document insists that proclaiming the Gospel and serving the poor are inseparable — a “Church which is poor and for the poor.”

The Catholic Funeral Rite

The Catholic funeral rite reflects the Church’s eschatological faith: death is not the end, but the beginning of the passage to eternal life. The rite typically has three stages: the Reception of the Body (at the church, with prayers and the placing of the coffin near the altar); the Requiem Mass (a full Mass in which the Paschal Mystery is re-presented and the deceased is commended to God); and the Committal (the burial or cremation, accompanied by prayers commending the soul to God’s mercy). The white pall placed over the coffin recalls the white garment of baptism, symbolising that the deceased belongs to Christ.

The funeral rite has been shaped by the Second Vatican Council’s renewal of liturgy. The “Preparing my funeral” initiative, promoted by the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales (endorsed by Vincent Nichols), encourages Catholics to plan their own funeral as an act of faith — choosing readings, prayers and music that express their personal faith and their hope in the resurrection.

Both Catholic and Protestant funerals affirm hope in the resurrection and commend the deceased to God. Key differences:

  • The Requiem Mass: The Catholic funeral includes a full Mass with the Eucharist at its centre; many Protestant funerals do not include the Eucharist. The Catholic rite explicitly re-presents the Paschal Mystery; Protestant services typically focus on Scripture, hymns and the preached word.
  • Prayer for the dead: Catholics pray for the deceased (particularly in connection with purgatory); most Protestant traditions do not pray for the dead, as they hold that the deceased go directly to their eternal destination.
  • The white pall: The baptismal symbolism of the pall is distinctly Catholic, linking death and resurrection to the sacramental initiation of baptism.
exam_tip_html: For “Outline three…” questions on Catholic Social Teaching, give three distinct points — for example: (1) CST is grounded in the preferential option for the poor; (2) CAFOD is the official agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, working in over forty countries; (3) Evangelii Gaudium (Pope Francis, 2013) calls the Church to go to the margins and prioritise the poor. For the 5-mark question, name a specific source: “Matthew 25:40 — ‘whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me’” or “Evangelii Gaudium (Pope Francis, 2013)” are both strong named sources. For 12-mark Discuss questions on mission, develop the alternative perspective — for example, some Christians argue that prioritising evangelism risks cultural imposition, while others argue that actions without words are insufficient. The alternative view must be as fully argued as the main one. SPaG rewards correct spelling of Evangelii Gaudium, subsidiarity and CAFOD.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic Social Teaching applies Gospel values to society; its scriptural foundation is Matthew 25:31–46 (Sheep and Goats), where Jesus identifies himself with the poor and vulnerable. CAFOD is the practical expression of CST in England and Wales.
  • Evangelii Gaudium (Pope Francis, 2013) calls the Church to be a missionary community that goes to the margins; mission and service of the poor are inseparable for Catholics.
  • The Catholic funeral rite includes three stages (reception, Requiem Mass, committal) and uses the white pall (recalling baptism) to express the Church’s hope in the resurrection; prayer for the dead reflects belief in purgatory.

practice_questions.text: Outline three principles of Catholic Social Teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete principle clearly identified. Acceptable points:
• The dignity of the human person — every person is made in God's image and deserves to be treated with respect.
• The preferential option for the poor — the most vulnerable have a first claim on society's resources and the Church's concern.
• Solidarity — all people are members of the human family and are responsible for one another.
• The common good — the conditions that allow all members of society to flourish.
• Subsidiarity — decisions should be taken at the lowest appropriate level, closest to those they affect.
[3 marks]

One mark per discrete point. Acceptable points:
• The Catholic funeral rite typically involves three stages: the Reception of the Body at the church, the Requiem Mass, and the Committal (burial or cremation).
• A white pall is placed over the coffin, recalling the white garment of baptism and symbolising hope in the resurrection.
• The Requiem Mass re-presents the Paschal Mystery and commends the deceased to God.
• Catholics pray for the dead at the funeral and afterwards, reflecting belief in purgatory.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Catholics put their belief in justice and peace into action.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per developed explanation.
• Catholics support CAFOD's work in over forty countries — through fundraising (Fast Days, parish giving), campaigning for fair trade and debt relief, and responding to humanitarian emergencies. This translates the Gospel command to love the neighbour into practical global action.
• Catholics apply Catholic Social Teaching's 'preferential option for the poor' in their local communities — through food banks, support of homeless shelters, and advocacy for just immigration policies. Cardinal Vincent Nichols has been an outspoken voice on poverty and the treatment of migrants, applying CST to British society.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic beliefs about mission and evangelism, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per explanation plus one mark for a named source.
• Catholics believe mission is a command given by Jesus himself — to go and make disciples of all nations. This is the Great Commission: the Church does not exist for itself but is sent into the world. Source: Matthew 28:19 — 'Go and make disciples of all nations.'
• Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium (2013) calls the Church to be a missionary community that goes to the margins and prioritises the poor — mission and service of the poor are inseparable. Source: Evangelii Gaudium, Pope Francis, 2013. (The fifth mark requires this named papal document with author and year; paraphrase without attribution does not earn it.)
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Helping the poor is more important than telling people about Jesus.'
Discuss this statement, giving arguments for and against, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; conclusion justifies a clear position with weighing.
Arguments in support: Matthew 25:31–46 (Sheep and Goats) suggests that serving the poor is a criterion of judgment — Jesus identifies himself with the vulnerable, so practical action is itself an encounter with Christ; CAFOD and CST show the Church taking this seriously; Evangelii Gaudium's 'Church which is poor and for the poor' prioritises deeds over words.
Arguments against: The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) explicitly commands making disciples and baptising — word and sacrament are not optional extras; Pope Francis in Evangelii Gaudium also insists that proclaiming the Gospel (not just social action) is the primary task; the Catholic understanding is that word and deed together constitute mission ('evangelisation' is both).
Conclusion must weigh and reach a position — e.g. most Catholic thinkers argue the two are inseparable, not in competition.
Secure (7–9): Both sides with some development; at least one source.
Developing (4–6): One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging (1–3): One-sided; no sources.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Evangelii Gaudium has influenced Catholic life.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per developed explanation.
• Evangelii Gaudium (Pope Francis, 2013) calls the Church to prioritise the poor and go to the margins of society. This has encouraged Catholic parishes to engage more actively with food banks, refugees and the homeless — turning inward-looking parish communities into missionary ones.
• Pope Francis's vision of a 'Church which is poor and for the poor' has renewed Catholic engagement with social justice campaigns, including CAFOD's advocacy on climate justice and fair trade, connecting everyday Catholic life to global structural change.
[4 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which papal document, issued by Pope Francis in 2013, calls the Church to be a 'missionary Church' that goes to the margins?
In the Sheep and Goats parable (Matthew 25:31–46), what does Jesus say about those who served the poor and vulnerable?
options: They earned their salvation through good works.
Whatever they did for the least of his brothers and sisters, they did for him.
They would be rewarded with material prosperity.
Their actions replaced the need for prayer and sacraments.

Match each Catholic Social Teaching principle to its meaning:
right: The most vulnerable have a first claim on the Church's concern
Decisions should be made at the lowest appropriate level
All people are members of one human family, responsible for each other

flashcard_questions.a: 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.'

flashcard_questions.q: What is CAFOD and who does it represent?
flashcard_questions.a: The Catholic Agency for Overseas Development — the official aid agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Evangelii Gaudium, and when was it issued?
flashcard_questions.a: Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation 'The Joy of the Gospel', issued in 2013.

flashcard_questions.a: That the Church must be 'poor and for the poor' and go to the margins rather than waiting for people to come to it.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three stages of the Catholic funeral rite?
flashcard_questions.a: Reception of the Body, Requiem Mass, and Committal (burial or cremation).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the white pall symbolise at a Catholic funeral?
flashcard_questions.a: The white garment of baptism — the deceased's belonging to Christ and hope of resurrection.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Catholics pray for the dead at a funeral?
flashcard_questions.a: Reflecting belief in purgatory — prayers may benefit those being purified before entering heaven.

flashcard_questions.q: Which encyclical, issued by Pope Leo XIII in 1891, began the modern tradition of Catholic Social Teaching?
flashcard_questions.a: Rerum Novarum — on workers' rights and the conditions of labour.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'preferential option for the poor' in CST?
flashcard_questions.a: The principle that the most vulnerable have a first claim on society's resources and the Church's concern.

glossary_terms.definition: A body of teaching developed by the Catholic Church from the late nineteenth century onwards that applies Gospel values to the structures of society, addressing poverty, justice, workers' rights and the common good.
The Catholic Agency for Overseas Development; the official overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, working to end poverty and promote justice worldwide.
Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation (2013) on the joy of the Gospel; it calls Catholics to go out to the margins of society and prioritise the poor.
The task given by Jesus to his followers to spread the Good News of the Gospel to all people and nations.
The active sharing of the Good News of Jesus Christ with those who have not heard it, with the goal of bringing them to faith.
The Archbishop of Westminster and the head of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, made a Cardinal by Pope Francis in 2014.
A white cloth laid over the coffin at a Catholic funeral, recalling the white garment of baptism; it symbolises the deceased's hope of resurrection.
